danish.title: Første bog (1805) — Kapitel 4
paragraphs: Netop da trådte endnu en gæst ind i salen: fyrst Andrej Bolkonskij, den lille fyrstindes mand. Han var en meget smuk ung mand af middelhøjde med faste, skarpt tegnede træk. Alt ved ham — fra hans trætte, kedede udtryk til hans rolige, afmålte gang — stod i den skarpeste kontrast til hans livlige lille hustru. Det var tydeligt, at han ikke blot kendte alle i salen, men fandt dem alle så trættende, at det udmattede ham at se på eller lytte til dem. Og af alle de ansigter, han fandt så kedelige, syntes intet at kede ham helt så meget som hans smukke kones. Han vendte sig fra hende med en grimasse, der skæmmede hans flotte ansigt, kyssede Anna Pavlovnas hånd og kiggede med sammenknebne øjne ud over hele selskabet.
»De drager i krig, fyrste?« sagde Anna Pavlovna.
[På fransk] »General Kutuzov« — sagde Bolkonskij på fransk med tryk på den sidste stavelse af generalens navn på fransk vis — »har været venlig nok til at tage mig som adjudant...«
»Og Lise, Deres hustru?«
»Hun tager på landet.«
»Skammer De Dem ikke over at berøve os Deres charmerende hustru?«

[På fransk] »André,« sagde hans kone og henvendte sig til sin mand i den samme kokette tone, hun brugte over for andre mænd, »vicomten har fortalt os den mest vidunderlige historie om Mademoiselle George og Bonaparte!«

Fyrst Andrej kneb øjnene sammen og vendte blikket bort. Pierre, der havde iagttaget ham med glade, hengivne øjne fra det øjeblik, han trådte ind, kom nu hen og tog hans arm. Før fyrst Andrej overhovedet nåede at se sig om, rynkede han atter panden — irriteret over, hvem der rørte ved hans arm — men da han så Pierres strålende ansigt, brød han ud i et uventet varmt og ægte smil.
»Nå, nå! Så du er også kommet ind i det fine selskab?« sagde han til Pierre.
»Jeg vidste, at du ville være her,« svarede Pierre. »Jeg kommer til middag hos dig. Må jeg?« tilføjede han med dæmpet stemme for ikke at forstyrre vicomten, der stadig fortalte sin historie.

»Nej, det kan ikke lade sig gøre!« sagde fyrst Andrej leende og trykkede Pierres hånd for at vise, at der ikke var nogen grund til at spørge. Han ville sige noget mere, men netop da rejste fyrst Vasilij og hans datter sig for at gå, og de to unge mænd rejste sig for at lade dem passere.

[På fransk] »De må undskylde mig, kære vicomte,« sagde fyrst Vasilij til franskmanden og holdt ham venligt i ærmet for at hindre ham i at rejse sig. »Denne elendige fest hos ambassadøren berøver mig en fornøjelse og tvinger mig til at afbryde Dem. Jeg er oprigtigt ked af at forlade Deres dejlige selskab,« sagde han og vendte sig mod Anna Pavlovna.

Hans datter, fyrstinde Hélène, passerede mellem stolene og samlede let folderne af sin kjole op, mens hendes smil strålede endnu mere på hendes smukke ansigt. Pierre stirrede på hende med fascinerede, næsten bange øjne, da hun fejede forbi ham.
»Meget smuk,« sagde fyrst Andrej.
»Bestemt,« sagde Pierre.

Idet fyrst Vasilij passerede, greb han Pierres hånd og sagde til Anna Pavlovna: »Tag Dem af denne bjørn for mig! Han har boet i mit hus en hel måned, og det er første gang, jeg ser ham ude i selskabet. Intet er så vigtigt for en ung mand som omgang med intelligente kvinder.«

Anna Pavlovna smilede og lovede at tage sig af Pierre. Hun vidste, at hans far var forbundet med fyrst Vasilij. Den ældre dame, der havde siddet ved den gamle tante, rejste sig hurtigt og skyndte sig efter fyrst Vasilij ud i forhallen. Al den kunstige interesse, hun havde vist, faldt fra hendes venlige, bekymrede ansigt, der nu kun udtrykte angst og frygt.
»Hvad med min søn Boris, fyrste?« sagde hun og fulgte ham ud i hallen. »Jeg kan ikke blive i Petersborg længere. Sig mig — hvilke nyheder kan jeg bringe hjem til min stakkels dreng?«

Selvom fyrst Vasilij lyttede modvilligt og temmelig uhøfligt til den ældre dame og endda viste tegn på utålmodighed, gav hun ham et underdanigt, bedende smil og greb hans hånd for at forhindre ham i at gå.
»Hvad ville det koste Dem at sige et ord til kejseren? Så ville han straks blive overført til garden,« sagde hun.

»Tro mig, fyrstinde, jeg er parat til at gøre alt, hvad jeg kan,« svarede fyrst Vasilij, »men det er vanskeligt for mig at bede kejseren. Jeg vil råde Dem til at gå gennem fyrst Golitsyn til Rumjantsev. Det ville være den bedste fremgangsmåde.«

Den ældre dame var fyrstinde Drubetskaja, fra en af de fineste familier i Rusland, men hun var fattig og havde været ude af selskabslivet så længe, at hun havde mistet alle sine gamle forbindelser. Hun var kommet til Petersborg udelukkende for at sikre en stilling i garden til sin eneste søn. Det var netop for at se fyrst Vasilij, at hun havde skaffet sig en invitation til Anna Pavlovnas selskab og havde siddet historien om vicomten igennem. Fyrst Vasilijs ord alarmerede hende; et bittert udtryk formørkede hendes engang smukke ansigt — men kun et øjeblik. Så smilede hun igen og greb fyrst Vasilijs arm endnu fastere.

»Hør mig, fyrste,« sagde hun. »Jeg har aldrig bedt Dem om noget, og jeg vil aldrig gøre det igen. Jeg har aldrig mindet Dem om min fars venskab med Dem. Men nu beder jeg Dem, for Guds skyld, gør dette for min søn — og jeg vil altid betragte Dem som min velgører,« tilføjede hun hurtigt. »Nej, bliv ikke vred — lov mig det bare! Jeg har allerede spurgt Golitsyn, og han sagde nej. Vær den hjertensvenlige mand, De altid har været,« sagde hun og forsøgte at smile, skønt der stod tårer i hendes øjne.
[På fransk] »Far, vi kommer for sent,« sagde fyrstinde Hélène og drejede sit smukke hoved og kiggede tilbage over sin skulpterede skulder, mens hun ventede ved døren.

Social indflydelse er imidlertid en form for kapital, der skal bruges med omhu, hvis den skal vare. Fyrst Vasilij forstod dette, og da han havde indset, at hvis han brugte sin indflydelse til fordel for alle, der kom og bad, ville han snart ikke have nogen tilbage til sig selv, var han blevet forsigtig med at bruge den. Men i fyrstinde Drubetskajas tilfælde, efter hendes anden appel, følte han noget nær et samvittighedsstik. Hun havde mindet ham om noget, der var fuldstændig sandt: han skyldte sin karrieres første skridt hendes far. Desuden kunne han se af hendes opførsel, at hun var en af de kvinder — mest mødre — som, når de først har sat sig noget i hovedet, ikke hviler, før de har fået, hvad de vil, og som er fuldt parate til at blive ved med at insistere dag efter dag, time efter time, og om nødvendigt lave scener. Denne sidste tanke bevægede ham.

[På fransk] »Min kære Anna Mikhajlovna,« sagde han i sin sædvanlige fortrolige, trætte tone, »det er næsten umuligt for mig at gøre, hvad De beder om. Men for at bevise min hengivenhed for Dem og min respekt for Deres fars minde vil jeg gøre det umulige. Deres søn vil blive overført til garden. Her er min hånd på det. Er De tilfreds?«
»Min kære velgører! Det var det, jeg ventede af Dem — jeg kendte Deres godhed!« Han vendte sig for at gå.

»Vent — bare én ting mere! Når han er blevet overført til garden...« Hun tøvede. »De er på god fod med Mikhail Ilarionovich Kutuzov... anbefal Boris til ham som adjudant! Så kan jeg være rolig, og så...«
Fyrst Vasilij smilede.

»Nej, det kan jeg ikke love. De aner ikke, hvordan Kutuzov bliver bestormet, siden han blev udnævnt til øverstkommanderende. Han fortalte mig selv, at enhver dame i Moskva har konspireret for at prakke sin søn på ham som adjudant.«
»Nej, men lov mig det! Jeg slipper Dem ikke! Min kære velgører...«
[På fransk] »Far,« sagde hans smukke datter i samme tone som før, »vi kommer for sent.«
[På fransk] »Nå, farvel da! Farvel! De hører hende?«
»Så i morgen taler De med kejseren?«
»Ja, helt sikkert. Men hvad angår Kutuzov — det lover jeg ikke.«

[På fransk] »Lov det, lov det, Vasilij!« råbte Anna Mikhajlovna, da han gik, med smilet fra en koket pige — som nok engang var faldet hende naturligt, men nu passede meget dårligt til hendes bekymrede ansigt.

Hun syntes at have glemt sin alder og brugte af gammel vane alle sine gamle kvindelige kunster. Men i det øjeblik fyrsten var væk, antog hendes ansigt igen sit tidligere kolde, kunstige udtryk. Hun vendte tilbage til gruppen, hvor vicomten stadig holdt sit foredrag, og lod atter som om hun lyttede, mens hun ventede på det rette øjeblik til at tage af sted. Hendes mission var fuldført.

english.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: Just then another guest entered the drawing room: Prince Andrei Bolkonski, the little princess's husband. He was a very handsome young man of medium height, with firm, sharply defined features. Everything about him — from his weary, bored expression to his quiet, measured stride — stood in the sharpest contrast to his lively little wife. It was clear that he not only knew everyone in the room but found them all so tiresome that it exhausted him to look at or listen to them. And of all the faces he found so tedious, none seemed to bore him quite as much as his pretty wife's. He turned away from her with a grimace that marred his handsome face, kissed Anna Pavlovna's hand, and squinting slightly, surveyed the entire company.
"You are off to the war, Prince?" said Anna Pavlovna.

[Speaking in French] "General Kutuzov" — said Bolkonski, speaking French and stressing the last syllable of the general's name in the French manner — "has been kind enough to take me on as an aide-de-camp..."
"And Lise, your wife?"
"She will go to the country."
"Aren't you ashamed to deprive us of your charming wife?"

[Speaking in French] "André," said his wife, addressing her husband in the same flirtatious way she spoke to other men, "the vicomte has been telling us the most wonderful story about Mademoiselle George and Bonaparte!"

Prince Andrei screwed up his eyes and looked away. Pierre, who had been watching him with glad, affectionate eyes from the moment he entered the room, now came up and took his arm. Before Prince Andrei could even look around, he frowned again — annoyed at whoever was touching his arm — but when he saw Pierre's beaming face, he broke into an unexpectedly warm and genuine smile.
"Well, well! So you've made it into high society too?" he said to Pierre.
"I knew you would be here," replied Pierre. "I'll come to supper with you. May I?" he added in a low voice, so as not to disturb the vicomte, who was still telling his story.

"No, impossible!" said Prince Andrei, laughing and squeezing Pierre's hand to show that there was no need to ask. He wanted to say something more, but just then Prince Vasili and his daughter stood up to leave, and the two young men rose to let them pass.

[Speaking in French] "You must excuse me, dear Vicomte," said Prince Vasili to the Frenchman, holding him by the sleeve in a friendly way to keep him from getting up. "This wretched party at the ambassador's is robbing me of a pleasure and forcing me to cut you short. I'm truly sorry to leave your delightful gathering," he said, turning to Anna Pavlovna.

His daughter, Princess Hélène, passed between the chairs, lightly gathering up the folds of her gown, her smile shining even more brilliantly on her beautiful face. Pierre gazed at her with fascinated, almost frightened eyes as she swept past him.
"Very lovely," said Prince Andrei.
"Very," said Pierre.

As he passed, Prince Vasili seized Pierre's hand and said to Anna Pavlovna, "Educate this bear for me! He's been staying at my house for a whole month and this is the first time I've seen him out in society. Nothing is as essential for a young man as the company of intelligent women."

Anna Pavlovna smiled and promised to take Pierre in hand. She knew his father was connected to Prince Vasili. The elderly lady who had been sitting with the old aunt rose quickly and hurried after Prince Vasili into the entrance hall. All the artificial interest she had been showing dropped away from her kind, careworn face, which now expressed nothing but anxiety and fear.
"What about my son Boris, Prince?" she said, following him into the hall. "I can't stay in Petersburg any longer. Tell me — what news can I bring back to my poor boy?"

Although Prince Vasili listened reluctantly and rather rudely to the elderly lady, even showing signs of impatience, she gave him a fawning, pleading smile and seized his hand to prevent him from leaving.
"What would it cost you to put in a word with the Emperor? Then he would be transferred to the Guards immediately," she said.

"Believe me, Princess, I'm prepared to do everything I can," answered Prince Vasili, "but it's difficult for me to petition the Emperor. I'd advise you to go through Prince Golitsyn to Rumyantsev. That would be the best approach."

The elderly lady was Princess Drubetskaya, from one of the finest families in Russia, but she was poor and had been out of society for so long that she had lost all her old connections. She had come to Petersburg for the sole purpose of securing a position in the Guards for her only son. In fact, it was specifically to see Prince Vasili that she had obtained an invitation to Anna Pavlovna's reception and had sat through the vicomte's story. Prince Vasili's words alarmed her; a bitter expression clouded her once-handsome face — but only for a moment. Then she smiled again and gripped Prince Vasili's arm even more tightly.

"Listen to me, Prince," she said. "I have never asked you for anything, and I never will again. I have never reminded you of my father's friendship with you. But now I beg you, for God's sake, do this for my son — and I shall always consider you my benefactor," she added quickly. "No, don't be angry — just promise me! I've already asked Golitsyn and he refused. Be the kindhearted man you have always been," she said, trying to smile though tears stood in her eyes.
[Speaking in French] "Papa, we're going to be late," said Princess Hélène, turning her beautiful head and glancing back over her sculpted shoulder as she waited by the door.

Social influence, however, is a form of capital that must be spent carefully if it is to last. Prince Vasili understood this, and having realized that if he used his influence on behalf of everyone who came asking, he would soon have none left for himself, he had become cautious about spending it. But in Princess Drubetskaya's case, after her second appeal, he felt something close to a pang of conscience. She had reminded him of something that was perfectly true: he owed his first steps in his career to her father. Moreover, he could see from her manner that she was one of those women — mostly mothers — who, once they have set their minds on something, will not rest until they get what they want, and are fully prepared to keep insisting day after day, hour after hour, and if necessary, to make scenes. This last thought moved him.

[Speaking in French] "My dear Anna Mikhaylovna," he said with his usual familiar, weary tone, "it's nearly impossible for me to do what you're asking. But to prove my devotion to you and my respect for your father's memory, I will do the impossible. Your son will be transferred to the Guards. Here is my hand on it. Are you satisfied?"
"My dear benefactor! This is what I expected from you — I knew your kindness!" He turned to go.

"Wait — just one more thing! When he's been transferred to the Guards..." She hesitated. "You're on good terms with Mikhail Ilarionovich Kutuzov... recommend Boris to him as an adjutant! Then I'll be at peace, and then..."
Prince Vasili smiled.

"No, that I can't promise. You have no idea how Kutuzov is being hounded since his appointment as Commander-in-Chief. He told me himself that every lady in Moscow has conspired to foist her son on him as an adjutant."
"No, but do promise! I won't let you go! My dear benefactor..."
[Speaking in French] "Papa," said his beautiful daughter in the same tone as before, "we're going to be late."
[Speaking in French] "Well, goodbye then! Goodbye! You hear her?"
"So tomorrow you'll speak to the Emperor?"
"Yes, definitely. But about Kutuzov — that I don't promise."

[Speaking in French] "Do promise, do promise, Vasili!" cried Anna Mikhaylovna as he left, wearing the smile of a flirtatious girl — which had probably once come naturally to her but was now very poorly suited to her careworn face.

She seemed to have forgotten her age, and out of long habit was employing all her old feminine wiles. But the moment the prince was gone, her face resumed its former cold, artificial expression. She went back to the group where the vicomte was still holding forth, and once again pretended to listen while she waited for the right moment to leave. Her mission was accomplished.
